title: Getting Beneath the Veil of Effective Schools: Evidence from New York City
research_question: Which characteristics and operational practices of schools actually drive their effectiveness at raising student achievement? In particular, do traditional resource-based inputs such as class size, per-pupil expenditure, and teacher credentials explain school effectiveness, or do practices such as teacher feedback, data-driven instruction, intensive tutoring, instructional time, and high expectations matter more?
data_description: The authors assembled an original dataset on 35 charter schools in New York City serving grades 3–8 during the 2009–2010 school year. School-level data were collected through principal interviews, teacher and student surveys, lesson plans across testable grades, full-day site visits, and videotaped classroom observations, capturing measures of teacher feedback frequency, professional development, interim assessments, differentiation, tutoring intensity, instructional time, school culture and disciplinary expectations, parental engagement, wrap-around services, and curricular rigor. These were merged with administrative data from the New York City Department of Education covering 2003–2004 through 2009–2010, including student race, gender, free/reduced-price lunch status, special education and English-language-learner status, attendance, behavior, and state math and ELA test scores in grades 3–8. Admissions lottery records were obtained from 22 oversubscribed schools, yielding 9,850 lottery applicants across 58 lotteries. An out-of-sample dataset covers 56 additional NYC charters using site-visit reports and state accountability documents.
institutional_context: Charter schools in New York City operate under state law with substantial autonomy over staffing, curriculum, schedule, and culture, but are publicly funded and required to admit students by random lottery when oversubscribed. They were established partly to act as laboratories for educational practices that could inform traditional public schools, and as a result they exhibit wide variation in pedagogical philosophies—ranging from arts-integrated models like the Bronx Charter School for the Arts to 'No Excuses' schools such as KIPP Infinity, the HCZ Promise Academies, and Democracy Prep, which emphasize extended school days and years, strict discipline, frequent assessment, and intensive focus on math and reading. Traditional NYC public schools, by contrast, typically meet 180 days per year for 6.0–7.5 hours daily under more standardized staffing and scheduling rules. This heterogeneity in inputs—combined with lottery-based admissions in oversubscribed schools—creates an unusually rich setting for linking specific school practices to measured effectiveness.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Attending effective schools in New York City positively impacts student achievement.
